introduction-the-missing-why.core: Code and infrastructure show what was built but not why. When the people who decided leave, the reasoning leaves with them: organisational amnesia.

first_principles.problem: You find Kubernetes on bare metal or a hand-rolled auth system and can't tell whether it was a smart constraint-driven choice or an accident. So teams either fear changing it or 'fix' it and re-learn the same lessons painfully.
truths: Artifacts outlive the people who made them.
Constraints and rejected options are invisible in code.
derivation: Capture **the why** at decision time, while context is fresh.
Record **constraints, alternatives and trade-offs**, not just the outcome.
Keep it **next to the code** so it's found when needed.

analogy.title: A house with no blueprints
analogy.story: A new owner finds a strange wall. Is it load-bearing? Without plans or notes, removing it is a gamble.
analogy.breaks: Walls can be inspected physically. Design reasons can't be recovered from code at all once forgotten.

example.title: The bare-metal cluster
example.scenario: A new SRE wants to move a cluster to a managed service.

steps.label: Lost context
steps.detail: Bare metal was chosen for a data-residency contract.

steps.label: With an ADR
steps.detail: The SRE would have read the constraint in two minutes.

example.outcome: you see why decisions need their reasons written down.

points: Write the why at decision time.

check.a: Losing the reasons behind past decisions, so teams can't tell whether to keep or change them.

the-architectural-decision-record-adr.core: An ADR is a short, immutable record of one significant decision: its context, the choice and its consequences, written when the decision is made.

first_principles.problem: 50-page design docs go stale immediately and nobody reads them. Teams need a lightweight, durable way to keep decision history.
truths: Small documents get written and read.
Decisions happen one at a time.
History is more trustworthy if not rewritten.
derivation: One ADR per **decision** (Nygard, 2011).
Keep it **short** (one or two pages).
Make it **immutable** once accepted; change by adding new ADRs.
Store in the **repo** next to the code.

analogy.title: A ship's logbook
analogy.story: Each entry records one event at the time it happened. Entries aren't edited later; corrections are new entries.
analogy.breaks: Logbooks record everything. ADRs are only for significant decisions, or they become noise.

example.title: Recording a database switch
example.scenario: The team moves the order service to Postgres.

steps.label: Write
steps.detail: Context, decision, consequences in one page.

example.outcome: future engineers find the decision and its reasons in seconds.

check.q: Why are ADRs immutable once accepted?
check.a: So the history of what was decided and why stays trustworthy; changes are recorded as new ADRs.

the-anatomy-of-an-adr.core: A good ADR has a title, status, date, and three pillars: Context (forces and constraints), Decision (what we'll do), and Consequences (the good and the bad we accept).

first_principles.problem: Free-form decision notes are hard to scan and often skip the crucial parts: the constraints at the time and the downsides accepted.
truths: Context explains why a choice was reasonable.
derivation: **Context**: the problem, constraints, data (e.g. two MongoDB outages, 8 h/week maintenance).
**Decision**: an active statement ("We will use RDS PostgreSQL").
**Consequences**: benefits *and* costs, and what follow-up work is needed.
Include **alternatives considered** and why they lost.

analogy.title: A doctor's case note
analogy.story: Symptoms and history (context), the treatment chosen (decision), expected effects and side-effects (consequences).
analogy.breaks: Medical notes follow regulations. ADR quality depends entirely on team habits, so use a template.

example.title: ADR-0007: Use RDS PostgreSQL for orders

steps.label: Context
steps.detail: Two outages last quarter, 8 h/week maintenance, small team.

steps.label: Consequences
steps.detail: + managed backups; − 3-week migration, higher monthly bill.

code.text:
# ADR-0007: Use Amazon RDS PostgreSQL for the Order Service
## Status
Accepted (2024-03-15)
## Context
Self-managed MongoDB: 2 outages last quarter, ~8 h/week maintenance.
## Decision
We will migrate the Order Service to Amazon RDS PostgreSQL.
## Consequences
+ Managed backups, patching, failover
- 3-week migration; ~$400/month more

example.outcome: a reader understands both why the choice made sense and what it cost.

check.a: They explain what was knowingly traded away, so future readers don't mistake an accepted cost for an oversight.

managing-adr-lifecycle-and-status.core: ADRs are never deleted or rewritten. Their status changes (Proposed → Accepted → Superseded/Deprecated) and new ADRs reference old ones, so the history of reasoning stays intact.

first_principles.problem: A decision that was right for 1,000 users may be wrong for 10 million. If you edit old ADRs to match today, you lose the record of how and why thinking evolved.
truths: The history of reasoning is valuable.
Readers need to know which decision is current.
derivation: Use **statuses**: Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Deprecated, Superseded.
To change a decision, **write a new ADR** that supersedes the old one.
Mark the old one '**Superseded by ADR-00XX**' and link both ways.

analogy.title: Laws and amendments
analogy.story: Old laws aren't erased; amendments repeal or replace them, and the record shows what was law when.
analogy.breaks: Legal codes are curated by staff. ADR links must be maintained by the team or tooling.

example.title: Self-hosted CI to managed CI
example.scenario: ADR-0003 (2020) chose self-hosted Jenkins to save money.

steps.label: New context
steps.detail: Jenkins upkeep now costs more than managed CI.

example.outcome: anyone can trace why the team moved and what was true at each point.

check.q: How do you change an accepted ADR?
check.a: Write a new ADR that supersedes it and update the old one's status to point to the new one.

tooling-for-adrs.core: ADRs can be plain Markdown in Git, but tools like adr-tools automate numbering, templates and superseding links, which removes friction so people keep writing them.

first_principles.problem: Manually finding the next number, copying the template and updating superseded records is tedious, and tedious habits die.
derivation: Keep ADRs in **docs/adr/** in Git.
Use **adr-tools** (`adr new`, `adr new -s 3`) to scaffold and supersede.
Generate an **index** so people can browse decisions.
Optionally render them in a docs site (Log4brains, Backstage).

analogy.title: A label printer
analogy.story: You could hand-write every file label, but a label printer makes it effortless, so files actually get labelled.
analogy.breaks: Labels don't need reviews. ADRs still need human judgement; tooling only removes the mechanics.

example.title: Superseding with one command
example.scenario: Replacing ADR-0003 with a new CI decision.

steps.label: Command
steps.detail: Creates 0021 with the template and a link to 0003.

code.text:
adr init docs/adr
adr new "Use RDS PostgreSQL for orders"
adr new -s 3 "Move CI from Jenkins to GitHub Actions"
adr list

example.outcome: writing an ADR takes seconds of setup, so it actually happens.

check.a: Creates a new ADR that supersedes ADR 3, linking them and updating ADR 3's status.

request-for-comments-rfcs.core: An RFC is a proposal written *before* deciding, to gather input on a significant, hard-to-reverse or cross-team change. ADRs record decisions; RFCs shape them.

first_principles.problem: Big changes made by one person surprise other teams, miss risks others could have spotted, and get relitigated later. Meetings don't scale and leave no record.
derivation: Use an RFC when the change is **hard to reverse**, **cross-team**, **expensive** or **novel**.
Write a **proposal with alternatives** and ask for comments.
Set a **deadline** and a decider.
Record the outcome as an **ADR**.

analogy.title: A planning application
analogy.story: Before building, you post plans publicly; neighbours and experts comment by a deadline, then the council decides.
analogy.breaks: Planning has legal process. RFCs work only if the team respects deadlines and doesn't reopen settled ones.

example.title: Moving CI from Jenkins to GitHub Actions

steps.label: Input
steps.detail: Security points out OIDC is needed instead of long-lived secrets.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: The plan includes OIDC; an ADR records the final choice.

example.outcome: a better decision with buy-in from the teams it affects.

points: Use for big, shared, irreversible changes.

check.a: An RFC proposes a change and collects input before deciding; an ADR records the decision once made.

the-anatomy-of-an-rfc.core: A strong RFC has a short summary, a problem statement with data, the proposal, alternatives considered, risks and rollout, open questions, reviewers and a decision deadline.

first_principles.problem: Vague proposals get vague feedback or none. Readers need to grasp the ask in a minute and find the details they care about quickly.
truths: Most readers only read the summary.
derivation: **Meta**: author, reviewers, status, deadline.
**Summary**: 2–3 sentences anyone understands.
**Problem**: with numbers (e.g. 15 h/week Jenkins upkeep).
**Proposal, alternatives, risks, rollout plan, open questions**.

analogy.title: A business case
analogy.story: A good business case opens with a one-paragraph ask, backs it with numbers, compares options and lists risks.
analogy.breaks: Business cases are about money. RFCs also need technical detail, so keep it skimmable with clear headings.

example.title: RFC-0003: Jenkins → GitHub Actions

steps.label: Summary
steps.detail: Cut maintenance, speed builds ~40%, align with GitHub.

steps.label: Rollout
steps.detail: Migrate one team first, then the rest over a quarter.

example.outcome: reviewers can give targeted feedback and the decision is quick.

check.q: Why include alternatives in an RFC?
check.a: To show the options were genuinely weighed and let reviewers challenge the comparison.

adrs-and-rfcs-in-practice-organizational.core: ADRs and RFCs stick when they're woven into existing workflows: required in PRs for significant changes, reviewed in short regular meetings, kept lightweight, and modelled by senior engineers.

first_principles.problem: Teams adopt ADRs enthusiastically, write three, and stop. Without hooks into daily work the practice fades.
truths: Habits survive when attached to existing workflows.
derivation: **PR gate**: changes to dependencies, data stores, pipelines or public APIs include an ADR.
**Architecture review**: 30 min biweekly on open RFCs and new ADRs.
**Keep it light**: one page is fine.
**Lead by example**: seniors write them too.

analogy.title: Flossing with brushing
analogy.story: Habits stick when attached to something you already do. Flossing right after brushing works better than flossing 'sometime'.
analogy.breaks: Dental habits are personal. ADR habits are social, so leadership modelling matters.

example.title: A PR adding Redis
example.scenario: A developer opens a PR that introduces Redis as a new dependency.

steps.label: Gate
steps.detail: The PR template asks if an ADR is needed.

steps.label: Review
steps.detail: Reviewers check the code and the reasoning together.

example.outcome: decision records become a natural by-product of shipping.

check.q: What's the most effective adoption mechanism?
check.a: Requiring an ADR in the same pull request for significant changes.
